title: My spell judge thought a welding spell couldn’t melt ice. How would you test for that?
author: vay_108
selftext:
I’m building Evergrowing Codex, a browser game where players write their own spells and try them in hand-written trials. One playtester tried to free an object from ice with a welding spell. The LLM judge refused because it thought the spell only worked on metal. The player had described what the beam was strong enough to do. The model read that as a restriction on what it could touch.

I’ve been splitting this into two questions. When you invent a spell, the game saves what the spell can do. When you cast it, the judge gets that saved effect, what you’re trying to do, and the current scene. A heat beam can heat ice if it can reach it. Whether it frees the object intact is a separate call.

I added two cases to the model checks that look almost identical. In one, the beam is hot enough to melt metal and should be able to melt the ice. In the other, the spell explicitly says it only transfers heat to steel, so the ice should be unaffected. Having both cases in the test makes it harder to fix one by just telling the model to always allow heat on ice.

If you’ve shipped a game with an LLM making calls like this, where did you draw the line between the model and ordinary code? I’m especially curious how you’d test that two wordings of the same action give the same result while a small change to the actual spell can still change the outcome.

[Here’s the game](https://evergrowing-codex.com/) if you want to see the setup.

comments.author: fued
comments.body: An arc welder wouldn't melt ice tho would it?

replies.author: vay_108
replies.body: Yeah, bad name on my part. It’s a magic heat beam. If it can reach the ice, it can melt it

comments.author: No-Pollution7797
comments.body:
I think the root of that bug is that "strong enough to melt metal" and "only works on metal" end up as the same kind of sentence in the saved effect. I'd have spell creation write the limits as their own explicit line, and if the player never said "only," the judge treats it as having no target restriction instead of inferring one from the example they gave.



For the wording test, I'd write three or four paraphrases of the same cast and run each several times, then compare how often each one passes rather than a single yes or no, since one run per case will flicker on its own. Your minimal pairs are the other half, and I'd keep adding one every time a playtester finds a new misread like this.

comments.author: biggdogg420
comments.body: I’d add a third part to that test: run both phrasings again with the ice behind a barrier. Both unrestricted forms should agree that the ice can’t be reached. If the game can already tell whether the beam has a clear path, give the judge that result so a wording change can’t accidentally change the geometry.
